## Make bed features for continuous bigwig outlier high or low value regions

For building some of the [NIH MARBL T2T assembly polishing](https://github.com/marbl/training) tools as Galaxy workflows for the VGP. Idea is to identify regions of very low or high coverage, or of sparse or dense dinucleotide repeat regions for example, as bed features that can be combined into a single, summary "issues" or "anomalies" track for a new (VGP or other) assembly. Bigwig regions as long or longer than `minwin` (10 works well) where all values are at or above (below) a defined quantile cutoff such as 0.99 (0.01) are written to a bed file. 

Both high and low features combined, and high-only/low-only bed files can be created. Multiple bigwigs can be combined and bed features have the provided bigwig label as annotation - only makes sense if they share the same reference so all the features can be displayed. 

The quantile cut point values are estimated and applied over each chromosome, then turned into contiguous regions of `minwin` length using a few lines of [borrowed numpy code](http://gregoryzynda.com/python/numpy/contiguous/interval/2019/11/29/contiguous-regions.html). Makes it look easy and is very fast.

Sample images below from the JBrowse2 tool and Arang's HG002 human assembly paternal haplotype. Wrote a new JB2 plugin to show bed feature scores high as red and low as blue, in the sample images below. 

Whole paternal chromosome 14 view - bigwig is top track, "issues" bed is lower track:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/cdee3a2b-ae31-4282-b744-992c15fb49db)

Zooming in to start of the chromosome, showing details of that long region of low coverage and peaks of high coverage:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/59d1564b-0c34-42a3-b437-44332cf1b2f0)

Some obvious differences in the red/blue bed region distributions between chromosomes 14,15,21,22 and Y in this "all contigs" view - explanations welcomed!

![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/162bf681-2977-4eb8-8d6f-9dad5b3931f8)

[pybigtools](https://github.com/jackh726/bigtools) is used for the bigwig interface. 

### Why not use DeepTools windowed mean values for this purpose?
bigwig coverage values have a very long right tail and look more like a poisson than a normal distribution so a  parametric approach is problematic for guaranteeing some level of control for type 1 errors (false positives) in the context of billions of bigwig values. Using an empirical windowed quantile cut-off this way, the probability of 10 consecutive values at or above a 99th centile cutoff by chance gives 0.01<sup>10</sup> as a generalisable false positive rate.

### Quantiles per chromosome rather than quantiles for the whole bigwig 
Not feasible to hold all contigs in the entire decoded bigwig in RAM to estimate quantiles. It may be
better to sample across all chromosomes so as not to lose any systematic differences between them - the current method will hide those differences unfortunately. Sampling might be possible. Looking at the actual quantile values across a couple of test bigwigs suggests that there is not much variation between chromosomes but there's an optional tabular report to check them for each input bigwig.

## Make bed features for continuous bigwig outlier high or low value regions

For building some of the [NIH MARBL T2T assembly polishing](https://github.com/marbl/training) tools as Galaxy workflows for the VGP. Idea is to identify regions of very low or high coverage, or of sparse or dense dinucleotide repeat regions for example, as bed features that can be combined into a single, summary "issues" or "anomalies" track for a new (VGP or other) assembly. Bigwig regions as long or longer than `minwin` (10 works well) where all values are at or above (below) a defined quantile cutoff such as 0.99 (0.01) are written to a bed file. 

Both high and low features combined, and high-only/low-only bed files can be created. Multiple bigwigs can be combined and bed features have the provided bigwig label as annotation - only makes sense if they share the same reference so all the features can be displayed. 

The quantile cut point values are estimated and applied over each chromosome, then turned into contiguous regions of `minwin` length using a few lines of [borrowed numpy code](http://gregoryzynda.com/python/numpy/contiguous/interval/2019/11/29/contiguous-regions.html). Makes it look easy and is very fast.

Sample images below from the JBrowse2 tool and Arang's HG002 human assembly paternal haplotype. Wrote a new JB2 plugin to show bed feature scores high as red and low as blue, in the sample images below. 

Whole paternal chromosome 14 view - bigwig is top track, "issues" bed is lower track:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/cdee3a2b-ae31-4282-b744-992c15fb49db)

Zooming in to start of the chromosome, showing details of that long region of low coverage and peaks of high coverage:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/59d1564b-0c34-42a3-b437-44332cf1b2f0)

Some obvious differences in the red/blue bed region distributions between chromosomes 14,15,21,22 and Y in this "all contigs" view - explanations welcomed!

![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/162bf681-2977-4eb8-8d6f-9dad5b3931f8)

[pybigtools](https://github.com/jackh726/bigtools) is used for the bigwig interface. 

### Why not use DeepTools windowed mean values for this purpose?
bigwig coverage values have a very long right tail and look more like a poisson than a normal distribution so a  parametric approach is problematic for guaranteeing some level of control for type 1 errors (false positives) in the context of billions of bigwig values. Using an empirical windowed quantile cut-off this way, the probability of 10 consecutive values at or above a 99th centile cutoff by chance gives 0.01<sup>10</sup> as a generalisable false positive rate.

### Quantiles per chromosome rather than quantiles for the whole bigwig 
Not feasible to hold all contigs in the entire decoded bigwig in RAM to estimate quantiles. It may be
better to sample across all chromosomes so as not to lose any systematic differences between them - the current method will hide those differences unfortunately. Sampling might be possible. Looking at the actual quantile values across a couple of test bigwigs suggests that there is not much variation between chromosomes but there's an optional tabular report to check them for each input bigwig.

+"""
+Ross Lazarus June 2024 for VGP 
+Bigwigs are great, but hard to reliably "see" small low coverage or small very high coverage regions.
+Colouring in JB2 tracks will need a new plugin, so this code will find bigwig regions above and below a chosen percentile point.
+0.99 and 0.01 work well in testing with a minimum span of 10 bp.
+Multiple bigwigs **with the same reference** can be combined - bed segments will be named appropriately
+Combining multiple references works but is silly because only display will rely on one reference so others will not be shown...
+Tricksy numpy method from http://gregoryzynda.com/python/numpy/contiguous/interval/2019/11/29/contiguous-regions.html
+takes about 95 seconds for a 17MB test wiggle
+JBrowse2 bed normally displays ignore the score, so could provide separate low/high bed file outputs as an option.
+Update june 30 2024: wrote a 'no-build' plugin for beds to display red/blue if >0/<0 so those are used for scores
+Bed interval naming must be short for JB2 but needs input bigwig name and (lo or hi).
+"""
+import argparse
+import numpy as np
+import os
+import pybigtools
+import sys
+from pathlib import Path
+
+class findOut():
+
+    def __init__(self, args):
+        self.bwnames=args.bigwig
+        self.bwlabels=args.bigwiglabels
+        self.bedwin=args.minwin
+        self.qlo=args.qlo
+        self.qhi=args.qhi
+        self.bedouthilo=args.bedouthilo
+        self.bedouthi=args.bedouthi
+        self.bedoutlo=args.bedoutlo
+        self.tableoutfile = args.tableoutfile
+        self.bedwin = args.minwin
+        self.qhi = args.qhi
+        self.qlo = args.qlo
+        self.makeBed()
+
+    def processVals(self, bw, isTop):
+        # http://gregoryzynda.com/python/numpy/contiguous/interval/2019/11/29/contiguous-regions.html
+        if isTop:
+            bwex = np.r_[False, bw >= self.bwtop, False] # extend with 0s
+        else:
+            bwex = np.r_[False, bw <= self.bwbot, False]
+        bwexd = np.diff(bwex)
+        bwexdnz = bwexd.nonzero()[0]
+        bwregions = np.reshape(bwexdnz, (-1,2))
+        return bwregions
+
+    def writeBed(self, bed, bedfname):
+        """
+        potentially multiple
+        """
+        bed.sort()
+        beds = ['%s\t%d\t%d\t%s\t%d' % x for x in bed]
+        with open(bedfname, "w") as bedf:
+            bedf.write('\n'.join(beds))
+            bedf.write('\n')
+        print('Wrote %d bed regions to %s' % (len(bed), bedfname))
+
+    def makeBed(self):
+        bedhi = []
+        bedlo = []
+        bwlabels = self.bwlabels
+        bwnames = self.bwnames
+        print('bwnames=', bwnames, "bwlabs=", bwlabels)
+        restab = ["bigwig\tcontig\tn\tmean\tstd\tmin\tmax\tqtop\tqbot"]
+        for i, bwname in enumerate(bwnames):
+            bwlabel = bwlabels[i].replace(" ",'')
+            fakepath = 'in%d.bw' % i
+            if os.path.isfile(fakepath):
+              os.remove(fakepath)
+            p = Path(fakepath)
+            p.symlink_to( bwname ) # required by pybigtools (!)
+            bwf = pybigtools.open(fakepath)
+            chrlist = bwf.chroms()
+            chrs = list(chrlist.keys())
+            chrs.sort()
+            for chr in chrs:
+                bw = bwf.values(chr)
+                bw = bw[~np.isnan(bw)] # some have NaN if parts of a contig not covered
+                if self.qhi is not None:
+                    self.bwtop = np.quantile(bw, self.qhi)
+                    bwhi = self.processVals(bw, isTop=True)
+                    for i, seg in enumerate(bwhi):
+                        if seg[1] - seg[0] >= self.bedwin:
+                            bedhi.append((chr, seg[0], seg[1], '%s_hi' % (bwlabel), 1))
+                if self.qlo is not None:
+                    self.bwbot = np.quantile(bw, self.qlo)
+                    bwlo = self.processVals(bw, isTop=False)            
+                    for i, seg in enumerate(bwlo):
+                        if seg[1] - seg[0] >= self.bedwin:
+                            bedlo.append((chr, seg[0], seg[1], '%s_lo' % (bwlabel), -1))
+                bwmean = np.mean(bw)
+                bwstd = np.std(bw)
+                bwmax = np.max(bw)
+                nrow = np.size(bw)
+                bwmin = np.min(bw)
+                restab.append('%s\t%s\t%d\t%f\t%f\t%f\t%f\t%f\t%f' % (bwlabel,chr,nrow,bwmean,bwstd,bwmin,bwmax,self.bwtop,self.bwbot))  
+        stable = '\n'.join(restab)      
+        print(stable)
+        if self.tableoutfile:
+            with open(self.tableoutfile, 'w') as t:
+                t.write(stable)
+                t.write('\n')
+        if self.bedoutlo:
+            if self.qlo:
+                self.writeBed(bedlo, self.bedoutlo)
+        if self.bedouthi:
+            if self.qhi:
+                self.writeBed(bedhi, self.bedouthi)
+        if self.bedouthilo:
+            allbed = bedlo + bedhi
+            self.writeBed(allbed, self.bedouthilo)
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
+    a = parser.add_argument
+    a('-m', '--minwin',default=10, type=int)
+    a('-l', '--qlo',default=None, type=float)
+    a('-i', '--qhi',default=None, type=float)
+    a('-w', '--bigwig', nargs='+')
+    a('-n', '--bigwiglabels', nargs='+')
+    a('-o', '--bedouthilo', default=None, help="optional high and low combined bed")
+    a('-u', '--bedouthi', default=None, help="optional high only bed")
+    a('-b', '--bedoutlo', default=None, help="optional low only bed")
+    a('-t', '--tableoutfile', default=None)

## Make bed features for continuous bigwig outlier high or low value regions

For building some of the [NIH MARBL T2T assembly polishing](https://github.com/marbl/training) tools as Galaxy workflows for the VGP. Idea is to identify regions of very low or high coverage, or of sparse or dense dinucleotide repeat regions for example, as bed features that can be combined into a single, summary "issues" or "anomalies" track for a new (VGP or other) assembly. Bigwig regions as long or longer than `minwin` (10 works well) where all values are at or above (below) a defined quantile cutoff such as 0.99 (0.01) are written to a bed file. 

Both high and low features combined, and high-only/low-only bed files can be created. Multiple bigwigs can be combined and bed features have the provided bigwig label as annotation - only makes sense if they share the same reference so all the features can be displayed. 

The quantile cut point values are estimated and applied over each chromosome, then turned into contiguous regions of `minwin` length using a few lines of [borrowed numpy code](http://gregoryzynda.com/python/numpy/contiguous/interval/2019/11/29/contiguous-regions.html). Makes it look easy and is very fast.

Sample images below from the JBrowse2 tool and Arang's HG002 human assembly paternal haplotype. Wrote a new JB2 plugin to show bed feature scores high as red and low as blue, in the sample images below. 

Whole paternal chromosome 14 view - bigwig is top track, "issues" bed is lower track:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/cdee3a2b-ae31-4282-b744-992c15fb49db)

Zooming in to start of the chromosome, showing details of that long region of low coverage and peaks of high coverage:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/59d1564b-0c34-42a3-b437-44332cf1b2f0)

Some obvious differences in the red/blue bed region distributions between chromosomes 14,15,21,22 and Y in this "all contigs" view - explanations welcomed!

![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/162bf681-2977-4eb8-8d6f-9dad5b3931f8)

[pybigtools](https://github.com/jackh726/bigtools) is used for the bigwig interface. 

### Why not use DeepTools windowed mean values for this purpose?
bigwig coverage values have a very long right tail and look more like a poisson than a normal distribution so a  parametric approach is problematic for guaranteeing some level of control for type 1 errors (false positives) in the context of billions of bigwig values. Using an empirical windowed quantile cut-off this way, the probability of 10 consecutive values at or above a 99th centile cutoff by chance gives 0.01<sup>10</sup> as a generalisable false positive rate.

### Quantiles per chromosome rather than quantiles for the whole bigwig 
Not feasible to hold all contigs in the entire decoded bigwig in RAM to estimate quantiles. It may be
better to sample across all chromosomes so as not to lose any systematic differences between them - the current method will hide those differences unfortunately. Sampling might be possible. Looking at the actual quantile values across a couple of test bigwigs suggests that there is not much variation between chromosomes but there's an optional tabular report to check them for each input bigwig.

## Make bed features for continuous bigwig outlier high or low value regions

For building some of the [NIH MARBL T2T assembly polishing](https://github.com/marbl/training) tools as Galaxy workflows for the VGP. Idea is to identify regions of very low or high coverage, or of sparse or dense dinucleotide repeat regions for example, as bed features that can be combined into a single, summary "issues" or "anomalies" track for a new (VGP or other) assembly. Bigwig regions as long or longer than `minwin` (10 works well) where all values are at or above (below) a defined quantile cutoff such as 0.99 (0.01) are written to a bed file. 

Both high and low features combined, and high-only/low-only bed files can be created. Multiple bigwigs can be combined and bed features have the provided bigwig label as annotation - only makes sense if they share the same reference so all the features can be displayed. 

The quantile cut point values are estimated and applied over each chromosome, then turned into contiguous regions of `minwin` length using a few lines of [borrowed numpy code](http://gregoryzynda.com/python/numpy/contiguous/interval/2019/11/29/contiguous-regions.html). Makes it look easy and is very fast.

Sample images below from the JBrowse2 tool and Arang's HG002 human assembly paternal haplotype. Wrote a new JB2 plugin to show bed feature scores high as red and low as blue, in the sample images below. 

Whole paternal chromosome 14 view - bigwig is top track, "issues" bed is lower track:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/cdee3a2b-ae31-4282-b744-992c15fb49db)

Zooming in to start of the chromosome, showing details of that long region of low coverage and peaks of high coverage:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/59d1564b-0c34-42a3-b437-44332cf1b2f0)

Some obvious differences in the red/blue bed region distributions between chromosomes 14,15,21,22 and Y in this "all contigs" view - explanations welcomed!

![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/162bf681-2977-4eb8-8d6f-9dad5b3931f8)

[pybigtools](https://github.com/jackh726/bigtools) is used for the bigwig interface. 

### Why not use DeepTools windowed mean values for this purpose?
bigwig coverage values have a very long right tail and look more like a poisson than a normal distribution so a  parametric approach is problematic for guaranteeing some level of control for type 1 errors (false positives) in the context of billions of bigwig values. Using an empirical windowed quantile cut-off this way, the probability of 10 consecutive values at or above a 99th centile cutoff by chance gives 0.01<sup>10</sup> as a generalisable false positive rate.

### Quantiles per chromosome rather than quantiles for the whole bigwig 
Not feasible to hold all contigs in the entire decoded bigwig in RAM to estimate quantiles. It may be
better to sample across all chromosomes so as not to lose any systematic differences between them - the current method will hide those differences unfortunately. Sampling might be possible. Looking at the actual quantile values across a couple of test bigwigs suggests that there is not much variation between chromosomes but there's an optional tabular report to check them for each input bigwig.

+"""
+Ross Lazarus June 2024 for VGP 
+Bigwigs are great, but hard to reliably "see" small low coverage or small very high coverage regions.
+Colouring in JB2 tracks will need a new plugin, so this code will find bigwig regions above and below a chosen percentile point.
+0.99 and 0.01 work well in testing with a minimum span of 10 bp.
+Multiple bigwigs **with the same reference** can be combined - bed segments will be named appropriately
+Combining multiple references works but is silly because only display will rely on one reference so others will not be shown...
+Tricksy numpy method from http://gregoryzynda.com/python/numpy/contiguous/interval/2019/11/29/contiguous-regions.html
+takes about 95 seconds for a 17MB test wiggle
+JBrowse2 bed normally displays ignore the score, so could provide separate low/high bed file outputs as an option.
+Update june 30 2024: wrote a 'no-build' plugin for beds to display red/blue if >0/<0 so those are used for scores
+Bed interval naming must be short for JB2 but needs input bigwig name and (lo or hi).
+"""
+import argparse
+import numpy as np
+import os
+import pybigtools
+import sys
+from pathlib import Path
+
+class findOut():
+
+    def __init__(self, args):
+        self.bwnames=args.bigwig
+        self.bwlabels=args.bigwiglabels
+        self.bedwin=args.minwin
+        self.qlo=args.qlo
+        self.qhi=args.qhi
+        self.bedouthilo=args.bedouthilo
+        self.bedouthi=args.bedouthi
+        self.bedoutlo=args.bedoutlo
+        self.tableoutfile = args.tableoutfile
+        self.bedwin = args.minwin
+        self.qhi = args.qhi
+        self.qlo = args.qlo
+        self.makeBed()
+
+    def processVals(self, bw, isTop):
+        # http://gregoryzynda.com/python/numpy/contiguous/interval/2019/11/29/contiguous-regions.html
+        if isTop:
+            bwex = np.r_[False, bw >= self.bwtop, False] # extend with 0s
+        else:
+            bwex = np.r_[False, bw <= self.bwbot, False]
+        bwexd = np.diff(bwex)
+        bwexdnz = bwexd.nonzero()[0]
+        bwregions = np.reshape(bwexdnz, (-1,2))
+        return bwregions
+
+    def writeBed(self, bed, bedfname):
+        """
+        potentially multiple
+        """
+        bed.sort()
+        beds = ['%s\t%d\t%d\t%s\t%d' % x for x in bed]
+        with open(bedfname, "w") as bedf:
+            bedf.write('\n'.join(beds))
+            bedf.write('\n')
+        print('Wrote %d bed regions to %s' % (len(bed), bedfname))
+
+    def makeBed(self):
+        bedhi = []
+        bedlo = []
+        bwlabels = self.bwlabels
+        bwnames = self.bwnames
+        print('bwnames=', bwnames, "bwlabs=", bwlabels)
+        restab = ["bigwig\tcontig\tn\tmean\tstd\tmin\tmax\tqtop\tqbot"]
+        for i, bwname in enumerate(bwnames):
+            bwlabel = bwlabels[i].replace(" ",'')
+            fakepath = 'in%d.bw' % i
+            if os.path.isfile(fakepath):
+              os.remove(fakepath)
+            p = Path(fakepath)
+            p.symlink_to( bwname ) # required by pybigtools (!)
+            bwf = pybigtools.open(fakepath)
+            chrlist = bwf.chroms()
+            chrs = list(chrlist.keys())
+            chrs.sort()
+            for chr in chrs:
+                bw = bwf.values(chr)
+                bw = bw[~np.isnan(bw)] # some have NaN if parts of a contig not covered
+                if self.qhi is not None:
+                    self.bwtop = np.quantile(bw, self.qhi)
+                    bwhi = self.processVals(bw, isTop=True)
+                    for i, seg in enumerate(bwhi):
+                        if seg[1] - seg[0] >= self.bedwin:
+                            bedhi.append((chr, seg[0], seg[1], '%s_hi' % (bwlabel), 1))
+                if self.qlo is not None:
+                    self.bwbot = np.quantile(bw, self.qlo)
+                    bwlo = self.processVals(bw, isTop=False)            
+                    for i, seg in enumerate(bwlo):
+                        if seg[1] - seg[0] >= self.bedwin:
+                            bedlo.append((chr, seg[0], seg[1], '%s_lo' % (bwlabel), -1))
+                bwmean = np.mean(bw)
+                bwstd = np.std(bw)
+                bwmax = np.max(bw)
+                nrow = np.size(bw)
+                bwmin = np.min(bw)
+                restab.append('%s\t%s\t%d\t%f\t%f\t%f\t%f\t%f\t%f' % (bwlabel,chr,nrow,bwmean,bwstd,bwmin,bwmax,self.bwtop,self.bwbot))  
+        stable = '\n'.join(restab)      
+        print(stable)
+        if self.tableoutfile:
+            with open(self.tableoutfile, 'w') as t:
+                t.write(stable)
+                t.write('\n')
+        if self.bedoutlo:
+            if self.qlo:
+                self.writeBed(bedlo, self.bedoutlo)
+        if self.bedouthi:
+            if self.qhi:
+                self.writeBed(bedhi, self.bedouthi)
+        if self.bedouthilo:
+            allbed = bedlo + bedhi
+            self.writeBed(allbed, self.bedouthilo)
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
+    a = parser.add_argument
+    a('-m', '--minwin',default=10, type=int)
+    a('-l', '--qlo',default=None, type=float)
+    a('-i', '--qhi',default=None, type=float)
+    a('-w', '--bigwig', nargs='+')
+    a('-n', '--bigwiglabels', nargs='+')
+    a('-o', '--bedouthilo', default=None, help="optional high and low combined bed")
+    a('-u', '--bedouthi', default=None, help="optional high only bed")
+    a('-b', '--bedoutlo', default=None, help="optional low only bed")
+    a('-t', '--tableoutfile', default=None)
+    args = parser.parse_args()
+    print('args=', args)
+    if not (args.bedouthilo or args.bedouthi or args.bedoutlo):
+        sys.stderr.write("bigwig_outlier_bed.py cannot usefully run - need a bed output choice - must be one of low only, high only or both combined")
+        sys.exit(2)
+    if not (args.qlo or args.qhi):
+        sys.stderr.write("bigwig_outlier_bed.py cannot usefully run - need one or both of quantile cutpoints qhi and qlo")
+        sys.exit(2)
+    findOut(args)
+#end raw]]></configfile>

## Make bed features for continuous bigwig outlier high or low value regions

For building some of the [NIH MARBL T2T assembly polishing](https://github.com/marbl/training) tools as Galaxy workflows for the VGP. Idea is to identify regions of very low or high coverage, or of sparse or dense dinucleotide repeat regions for example, as bed features that can be combined into a single, summary "issues" or "anomalies" track for a new (VGP or other) assembly. Bigwig regions as long or longer than `minwin` (10 works well) where all values are at or above (below) a defined quantile cutoff such as 0.99 (0.01) are written to a bed file. 

Both high and low features combined, and high-only/low-only bed files can be created. Multiple bigwigs can be combined and bed features have the provided bigwig label as annotation - only makes sense if they share the same reference so all the features can be displayed. 

The quantile cut point values are estimated and applied over each chromosome, then turned into contiguous regions of `minwin` length using a few lines of [borrowed numpy code](http://gregoryzynda.com/python/numpy/contiguous/interval/2019/11/29/contiguous-regions.html). Makes it look easy and is very fast.

Sample images below from the JBrowse2 tool and Arang's HG002 human assembly paternal haplotype. Wrote a new JB2 plugin to show bed feature scores high as red and low as blue, in the sample images below. 

Whole paternal chromosome 14 view - bigwig is top track, "issues" bed is lower track:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/cdee3a2b-ae31-4282-b744-992c15fb49db)

Zooming in to start of the chromosome, showing details of that long region of low coverage and peaks of high coverage:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/59d1564b-0c34-42a3-b437-44332cf1b2f0)

Some obvious differences in the red/blue bed region distributions between chromosomes 14,15,21,22 and Y in this "all contigs" view - explanations welcomed!

![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/162bf681-2977-4eb8-8d6f-9dad5b3931f8)

[pybigtools](https://github.com/jackh726/bigtools) is used for the bigwig interface. 

### Why not use DeepTools windowed mean values for this purpose?
bigwig coverage values have a very long right tail and look more like a poisson than a normal distribution so a  parametric approach is problematic for guaranteeing some level of control for type 1 errors (false positives) in the context of billions of bigwig values. Using an empirical windowed quantile cut-off this way, the probability of 10 consecutive values at or above a 99th centile cutoff by chance gives 0.01<sup>10</sup> as a generalisable false positive rate.

### Quantiles per chromosome rather than quantiles for the whole bigwig 
Not feasible to hold all contigs in the entire decoded bigwig in RAM to estimate quantiles. It may be
better to sample across all chromosomes so as not to lose any systematic differences between them - the current method will hide those differences unfortunately. Sampling might be possible. Looking at the actual quantile values across a couple of test bigwigs suggests that there is not much variation between chromosomes but there's an optional tabular report to check them for each input bigwig.

## Make bed features for continuous bigwig outlier high or low value regions

For building some of the [NIH MARBL T2T assembly polishing](https://github.com/marbl/training) tools as Galaxy workflows for the VGP. Idea is to identify regions of very low or high coverage, or of sparse or dense dinucleotide repeat regions for example, as bed features that can be combined into a single, summary "issues" or "anomalies" track for a new (VGP or other) assembly. Bigwig regions as long or longer than `minwin` (10 works well) where all values are at or above (below) a defined quantile cutoff such as 0.99 (0.01) are written to a bed file. 

Both high and low features combined, and high-only/low-only bed files can be created. Multiple bigwigs can be combined and bed features have the provided bigwig label as annotation - only makes sense if they share the same reference so all the features can be displayed. 

The quantile cut point values are estimated and applied over each chromosome, then turned into contiguous regions of `minwin` length using a few lines of [borrowed numpy code](http://gregoryzynda.com/python/numpy/contiguous/interval/2019/11/29/contiguous-regions.html). Makes it look easy and is very fast.

Sample images below from the JBrowse2 tool and Arang's HG002 human assembly paternal haplotype. Wrote a new JB2 plugin to show bed feature scores high as red and low as blue, in the sample images below. 

Whole paternal chromosome 14 view - bigwig is top track, "issues" bed is lower track:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/cdee3a2b-ae31-4282-b744-992c15fb49db)

Zooming in to start of the chromosome, showing details of that long region of low coverage and peaks of high coverage:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/59d1564b-0c34-42a3-b437-44332cf1b2f0)

Some obvious differences in the red/blue bed region distributions between chromosomes 14,15,21,22 and Y in this "all contigs" view - explanations welcomed!

![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/162bf681-2977-4eb8-8d6f-9dad5b3931f8)

[pybigtools](https://github.com/jackh726/bigtools) is used for the bigwig interface. 

### Why not use DeepTools windowed mean values for this purpose?
bigwig coverage values have a very long right tail and look more like a poisson than a normal distribution so a  parametric approach is problematic for guaranteeing some level of control for type 1 errors (false positives) in the context of billions of bigwig values. Using an empirical windowed quantile cut-off this way, the probability of 10 consecutive values at or above a 99th centile cutoff by chance gives 0.01<sup>10</sup> as a generalisable false positive rate.

### Quantiles per chromosome rather than quantiles for the whole bigwig 
Not feasible to hold all contigs in the entire decoded bigwig in RAM to estimate quantiles. It may be
better to sample across all chromosomes so as not to lose any systematic differences between them - the current method will hide those differences unfortunately. Sampling might be possible. Looking at the actual quantile values across a couple of test bigwigs suggests that there is not much variation between chromosomes but there's an optional tabular report to check them for each input bigwig.

## Make bed features for continuous bigwig outlier high or low value regions

For building some of the [NIH MARBL T2T assembly polishing](https://github.com/marbl/training) tools as Galaxy workflows for the VGP. Idea is to identify regions of very low or high coverage, or of sparse or dense dinucleotide repeat regions for example, as bed features that can be combined into a single, summary "issues" or "anomalies" track for a new (VGP or other) assembly. Bigwig regions as long or longer than `minwin` (10 works well) where all values are at or above (below) a defined quantile cutoff such as 0.99 (0.01) are written to a bed file. 

Both high and low features combined, and high-only/low-only bed files can be created. Multiple bigwigs can be combined and bed features have the provided bigwig label as annotation - only makes sense if they share the same reference so all the features can be displayed. 

The quantile cut point values are estimated and applied over each chromosome, then turned into contiguous regions of `minwin` length using a few lines of [borrowed numpy code](http://gregoryzynda.com/python/numpy/contiguous/interval/2019/11/29/contiguous-regions.html). Makes it look easy and is very fast.

Sample images below from the JBrowse2 tool and Arang's HG002 human assembly paternal haplotype. Wrote a new JB2 plugin to show bed feature scores high as red and low as blue, in the sample images below. 

Whole paternal chromosome 14 view - bigwig is top track, "issues" bed is lower track:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/cdee3a2b-ae31-4282-b744-992c15fb49db)

Zooming in to start of the chromosome, showing details of that long region of low coverage and peaks of high coverage:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/59d1564b-0c34-42a3-b437-44332cf1b2f0)

Some obvious differences in the red/blue bed region distributions between chromosomes 14,15,21,22 and Y in this "all contigs" view - explanations welcomed!

![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/162bf681-2977-4eb8-8d6f-9dad5b3931f8)

[pybigtools](https://github.com/jackh726/bigtools) is used for the bigwig interface. 

### Why not use DeepTools windowed mean values for this purpose?
bigwig coverage values have a very long right tail and look more like a poisson than a normal distribution so a  parametric approach is problematic for guaranteeing some level of control for type 1 errors (false positives) in the context of billions of bigwig values. Using an empirical windowed quantile cut-off this way, the probability of 10 consecutive values at or above a 99th centile cutoff by chance gives 0.01<sup>10</sup> as a generalisable false positive rate.

### Quantiles per chromosome rather than quantiles for the whole bigwig 
Not feasible to hold all contigs in the entire decoded bigwig in RAM to estimate quantiles. It may be
better to sample across all chromosomes so as not to lose any systematic differences between them - the current method will hide those differences unfortunately. Sampling might be possible. Looking at the actual quantile values across a couple of test bigwigs suggests that there is not much variation between chromosomes but there's an optional tabular report to check them for each input bigwig.

## Make bed features for continuous bigwig outlier high or low value regions

For building some of the [NIH MARBL T2T assembly polishing](https://github.com/marbl/training) tools as Galaxy workflows for the VGP. Idea is to identify regions of very low or high coverage, or of sparse or dense dinucleotide repeat regions for example, as bed features that can be combined into a single, summary "issues" or "anomalies" track for a new (VGP or other) assembly. Bigwig regions as long or longer than `minwin` (10 works well) where all values are at or above (below) a defined quantile cutoff such as 0.99 (0.01) are written to a bed file. 

Both high and low features combined, and high-only/low-only bed files can be created. Multiple bigwigs can be combined and bed features have the provided bigwig label as annotation - only makes sense if they share the same reference so all the features can be displayed. 

The quantile cut point values are estimated and applied over each chromosome, then turned into contiguous regions of `minwin` length using a few lines of [borrowed numpy code](http://gregoryzynda.com/python/numpy/contiguous/interval/2019/11/29/contiguous-regions.html). Makes it look easy and is very fast.

Sample images below from the JBrowse2 tool and Arang's HG002 human assembly paternal haplotype. Wrote a new JB2 plugin to show bed feature scores high as red and low as blue, in the sample images below. 

Whole paternal chromosome 14 view - bigwig is top track, "issues" bed is lower track:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/cdee3a2b-ae31-4282-b744-992c15fb49db)

Zooming in to start of the chromosome, showing details of that long region of low coverage and peaks of high coverage:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/59d1564b-0c34-42a3-b437-44332cf1b2f0)

Some obvious differences in the red/blue bed region distributions between chromosomes 14,15,21,22 and Y in this "all contigs" view - explanations welcomed!

![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/162bf681-2977-4eb8-8d6f-9dad5b3931f8)

[pybigtools](https://github.com/jackh726/bigtools) is used for the bigwig interface. 

### Why not use DeepTools windowed mean values for this purpose?
bigwig coverage values have a very long right tail and look more like a poisson than a normal distribution so a  parametric approach is problematic for guaranteeing some level of control for type 1 errors (false positives) in the context of billions of bigwig values. Using an empirical windowed quantile cut-off this way, the probability of 10 consecutive values at or above a 99th centile cutoff by chance gives 0.01<sup>10</sup> as a generalisable false positive rate. See warning about the low cutoff in sparse truncated distributions such as coverage

### Quantiles per chromosome rather than quantiles for the whole bigwig 
Not feasible to hold all contigs in the entire decoded bigwig in RAM to estimate quantiles. It may be
better to sample across all chromosomes so as not to lose any systematic differences between them - the current method will hide those differences unfortunately. Sampling might be possible. Looking at the actual quantile values across a couple of test bigwigs suggests that there is not much variation between chromosomes but there's an optional tabular report to check them for each input bigwig.

Both high and low features combined, and high-only/low-only bed files can be created. Multiple bigwigs can be combined and bed features have the provided bigwig label as annotation - only makes sense if they share the same reference so all the features can be displayed. 

The quantile cut point values are estimated and applied over each chromosome, then turned into contiguous regions of `minwin` length using a few lines of [borrowed numpy code](http://gregoryzynda.com/python/numpy/contiguous/interval/2019/11/29/contiguous-regions.html). Makes it look easy and is very fast.

Sample images below from the JBrowse2 tool and Arang's HG002 human assembly paternal haplotype. Wrote a new JB2 plugin to show bed feature scores high as red and low as blue, in the sample images below. 

Whole paternal chromosome 14 view - bigwig is top track, "issues" bed is lower track:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/cdee3a2b-ae31-4282-b744-992c15fb49db)

Zooming in to start of the chromosome, showing details of that long region of low coverage and peaks of high coverage:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/59d1564b-0c34-42a3-b437-44332cf1b2f0)

Some obvious differences in the red/blue bed region distributions between chromosomes 14,15,21,22 and Y in this "all contigs" view - explanations welcomed!

![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/162bf681-2977-4eb8-8d6f-9dad5b3931f8)

[pybigtools](https://github.com/jackh726/bigtools) is used for the bigwig interface. 

### Why not use DeepTools windowed mean values for this purpose?
bigwig coverage values have a very long right tail and look more like a poisson than a normal distribution so a  parametric approach is problematic for guaranteeing some level of control for type 1 errors (false positives) in the context of billions of bigwig values. Using an empirical windowed quantile cut-off this way, the probability of 10 consecutive values at or above a 99th centile cutoff by chance gives 0.01<sup>10</sup> as a generalisable false positive rate. See warning about the low cutoff in sparse truncated distributions such as coverage

### Quantiles per chromosome rather than quantiles for the whole bigwig 
Not feasible to hold all contigs in the entire decoded bigwig in RAM to estimate quantiles. It may be
better to sample across all chromosomes so as not to lose any systematic differences between them - the current method will hide those differences unfortunately. Sampling might be possible. Looking at the actual quantile values across a couple of test bigwigs suggests that there is not much variation between chromosomes but there's an optional tabular report to check them for each input bigwig.

## Make bed features for continuous bigwig outlier high or low value regions

For building some of the [NIH MARBL T2T assembly polishing](https://github.com/marbl/training) tools as Galaxy workflows for the VGP. Idea is to identify regions of very low or high coverage, or of sparse or dense dinucleotide repeat regions for example, as bed features that can be combined into a single, summary "issues" or "anomalies" track for a new (VGP or other) assembly. Bigwig regions as long or longer than `minwin` (10 works well) where all values are at or above (below) a defined quantile cutoff such as 0.99 (0.01) are written to a bed file. 

Both high and low features combined, and high-only/low-only bed files can be created. Multiple bigwigs can be combined and bed features have the provided bigwig label as annotation - only makes sense if they share the same reference so all the features can be displayed. 

The quantile cut point values are estimated and applied over each chromosome, then turned into contiguous regions of `minwin` length using a few lines of [borrowed numpy code](http://gregoryzynda.com/python/numpy/contiguous/interval/2019/11/29/contiguous-regions.html). Makes it look easy and is very fast.

Sample images below from the JBrowse2 tool and Arang's HG002 human assembly paternal haplotype. Wrote a new JB2 plugin to show bed feature scores high as red and low as blue, in the sample images below. 

Whole paternal chromosome 14 view - bigwig is top track, "issues" bed is lower track:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/cdee3a2b-ae31-4282-b744-992c15fb49db)

Zooming in to start of the chromosome, showing details of that long region of low coverage and peaks of high coverage:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/59d1564b-0c34-42a3-b437-44332cf1b2f0)

Some obvious differences in the red/blue bed region distributions between chromosomes 14,15,21,22 and Y in this "all contigs" view - explanations welcomed!

![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/162bf681-2977-4eb8-8d6f-9dad5b3931f8)

[pybigtools](https://github.com/jackh726/bigtools) is used for the bigwig interface. 

### Why not use DeepTools windowed mean values for this purpose?
bigwig coverage values have a very long right tail and look more like a poisson than a normal distribution so a  parametric approach is problematic for guaranteeing some level of control for type 1 errors (false positives) in the context of billions of bigwig values. Using an empirical windowed quantile cut-off this way, the probability of 10 consecutive values at or above a 99th centile cutoff by chance gives 0.01<sup>10</sup> as a generalisable false positive rate. See warning about the low cutoff in sparse truncated distributions such as coverage

### Quantiles per chromosome rather than quantiles for the whole bigwig 
Not feasible to hold all contigs in the entire decoded bigwig in RAM to estimate quantiles. It may be
better to sample across all chromosomes so as not to lose any systematic differences between them - the current method will hide those differences unfortunately. Sampling might be possible. Looking at the actual quantile values across a couple of test bigwigs suggests that there is not much variation between chromosomes but there's an optional tabular report to check them for each input bigwig.

## Make bed features for continuous bigwig outlier high or low value regions

For building some of the [NIH MARBL T2T assembly polishing](https://github.com/marbl/training) tools as Galaxy workflows for the VGP. Idea is to identify regions of very low or high coverage, or of sparse or dense dinucleotide repeat regions for example, as bed features that can be combined into a single, summary "issues" or "anomalies" track for a new (VGP or other) assembly. Bigwig regions as long or longer than `minwin` (10 works well) where all values are at or above (below) a defined quantile cutoff such as 0.99 (0.01) are written to a bed file. 

Both high and low features combined, and high-only/low-only bed files can be created. Multiple bigwigs can be combined and bed features have the provided bigwig label as annotation - only makes sense if they share the same reference so all the features can be displayed. 

The quantile cut point values are estimated and applied over each chromosome, then turned into contiguous regions of `minwin` length using a few lines of [borrowed numpy code](http://gregoryzynda.com/python/numpy/contiguous/interval/2019/11/29/contiguous-regions.html). Makes it look easy and is very fast.

Sample images below from the JBrowse2 tool and Arang's HG002 human assembly paternal haplotype. Wrote a new JB2 plugin to show bed feature scores high as red and low as blue, in the sample images below. 

Whole paternal chromosome 14 view - bigwig is top track, "issues" bed is lower track:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/cdee3a2b-ae31-4282-b744-992c15fb49db)

Zooming in to start of the chromosome, showing details of that long region of low coverage and peaks of high coverage:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/59d1564b-0c34-42a3-b437-44332cf1b2f0)

Some obvious differences in the red/blue bed region distributions between chromosomes 14,15,21,22 and Y in this "all contigs" view - explanations welcomed!

![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/162bf681-2977-4eb8-8d6f-9dad5b3931f8)

[pybigtools](https://github.com/jackh726/bigtools) is used for the bigwig interface. 

### Why not use DeepTools windowed mean values for this purpose?
bigwig coverage values have a very long right tail and look more like a poisson than a normal distribution so a  parametric approach is problematic for guaranteeing some level of control for type 1 errors (false positives) in the context of billions of bigwig values. Using an empirical windowed quantile cut-off this way, the probability of 10 consecutive values at or above a 99th centile cutoff by chance gives 0.01<sup>10</sup> as a generalisable false positive rate. See warning about the low cutoff in sparse truncated distributions such as coverage

### Quantiles per chromosome rather than quantiles for the whole bigwig 
Not feasible to hold all contigs in the entire decoded bigwig in RAM to estimate quantiles. It may be
better to sample across all chromosomes so as not to lose any systematic differences between them - the current method will hide those differences unfortunately. Sampling might be possible. Looking at the actual quantile values across a couple of test bigwigs suggests that there is not much variation between chromosomes but there's an optional tabular report to check them for each input bigwig.

## Make bed features for continuous bigwig outlier high or low value regions

For building some of the [NIH MARBL T2T assembly polishing](https://github.com/marbl/training) tools as Galaxy workflows for the VGP. Idea is to identify regions of very low or high coverage, or of sparse or dense dinucleotide repeat regions for example, as bed features that can be combined into a single, summary "issues" or "anomalies" track for a new (VGP or other) assembly. Bigwig regions as long or longer than `minwin` (10 works well) where all values are at or above (below) a defined quantile cutoff such as 0.99 (0.01) are written to a bed file. 

Both high and low features combined, and high-only/low-only bed files can be created. Multiple bigwigs can be combined and bed features have the provided bigwig label as annotation - only makes sense if they share the same reference so all the features can be displayed. 

The quantile cut point values are estimated and applied over each chromosome, then turned into contiguous regions of `minwin` length using a few lines of [borrowed numpy code](http://gregoryzynda.com/python/numpy/contiguous/interval/2019/11/29/contiguous-regions.html). Makes it look easy and is very fast.

Sample images below from the JBrowse2 tool and Arang's HG002 human assembly paternal haplotype. Wrote a new JB2 plugin to show bed feature scores high as red and low as blue, in the sample images below. 

Whole paternal chromosome 14 view - bigwig is top track, "issues" bed is lower track:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/cdee3a2b-ae31-4282-b744-992c15fb49db)

Zooming in to start of the chromosome, showing details of that long region of low coverage and peaks of high coverage:
![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/59d1564b-0c34-42a3-b437-44332cf1b2f0)

Some obvious differences in the red/blue bed region distributions between chromosomes 14,15,21,22 and Y in this "all contigs" view - explanations welcomed!

![image](https://github.com/fubar2/bigwig_peak_bed/assets/6016266/162bf681-2977-4eb8-8d6f-9dad5b3931f8)

[pybigtools](https://github.com/jackh726/bigtools) is used for the bigwig interface. 

### Why not use DeepTools windowed mean values for this purpose?
bigwig coverage values have a very long right tail and look more like a poisson than a normal distribution so a  parametric approach is problematic for guaranteeing some level of control for type 1 errors (false positives) in the context of billions of bigwig values. Using an empirical windowed quantile cut-off this way, the probability of 10 consecutive values at or above a 99th centile cutoff by chance gives 0.01<sup>10</sup> as a generalisable false positive rate. See warning about the low cutoff in sparse truncated distributions such as coverage

### Quantiles per chromosome rather than quantiles for the whole bigwig 
Not feasible to hold all contigs in the entire decoded bigwig in RAM to estimate quantiles. It may be
better to sample across all chromosomes so as not to lose any systematic differences between them - the current method will hide those differences unfortunately. Sampling might be possible. {"action":"opened","number":6145,"pull_request":{"url":"https://api.github.com/repos/galaxyproject/tools-iuc/pulls/6145","id":1967603920,"node_id":"PR_kwDOAW4Y0s51R0DQ","html_url":"https://github.com/galaxyproject/tools-iuc/pull/6145","diff_url":"https://github.com/galaxyproject/tools-iuc/pull/6145.diff","patch_url":"https://github.com/galaxyproject/tools-iuc/pull/6145.patch","issue_url":"https://api.github.com/repos/galaxyproject/tools-iuc/issues/6145","number":6145,"state":"open","locked":false,"title":"Microsatbed: new tool for reporting short tandem repeats as bed track features.","user":{"login":"fubar2","id":6016266,"node_id":"MDQ6VXNlcjYwMTYyNjY=","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/6016266?v=4","gravatar_id":"","url":"https://api.github.com/users/fubar2","html_url":"https://github.com/fubar2","followers_url":"https://api.github.com/users/fubar2/followers","following_url":"https://api.github.com/users/fubar2/following{/other_user}","gists_url":"https://api.github.com/users/fubar2/gists{/gist_id}","starred_url":"https://api.github.com/users/fubar2/starred{/owner}{/repo}","subscriptions_url":"https://api.github.com/users/fubar2/subscriptions","organizations_url":"https://api.github.com/users/fubar2/orgs","repos_url":"https://api.github.com/users/fubar2/repos","events_url":"https://api.github.com/users/fubar2/events{/privacy}","received_events_url":"https://api.github.com/users/fubar2/received_events","type":"User","site_admin":false},"body":"FOR CONTRIBUTOR:
* [X] I have read the [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/galaxyproject/tools-iuc/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md) document and this tool is appropriate for the tools-iuc repo.
* [X] License permits unrestricted use (educational + commercial)
* [X] This PR adds a new tool or tool collection

This PR proposes a new tool, to help recreate some of the [NIH MARBL T2T assembly polishing](https://github.com/marbl/training) browser tracks in Galaxy workflows for the VGP. 

Those tracks display the density of specific dinucleotides such as `CG` in 128nt windows to help identify problematic regions, where they are over-represented, and may introduce technical errors in alignment for different kinds of sequencing methods. These are not *strictly* short tandem *repeats* because the MARBL code does not require any repetition - a single `CG` will be counted in each window together with any number of sequential repeats such as `CGCGCG` , so the primary use case allows any number of repeats (including singletons so zero repeats) of one or more specific motifs to be reported as features in a bed file. These will be converted to bigwigs and then back to bed files containing *issues* such as the highest and lowest extremes of dinucleotide density with the [bigwig value outlier](https://github.com/galaxyproject/tools-iuc/tree/main/tools/bigwig_outlier_bed) tool.

More generically, all motifs of specific size(s) from 1-6nt,  with any number of sequential repeats can be reported, allowing the tool to be used for visualising short tandem repeats and other kinds of true microsatellites.

#### This PR proposes a new tool and suggestions from anyone interested in microsatellites and STRs would be welcomed

Motivation was to recreate some of the [NIH MARBL T2T assembly polishing](https://github.com/marbl/training) browser tracks in Galaxy workflows for the VGP. Those tracks display the density of specific dinucleotides such as `CG` in 128nt windows to help identify problematic regions, where they are over-represented, and may introduce technical errors in alignment for different kinds of sequencing methods. 

The tool can be configured to output all motifs of one or more lengths from 1-6nt.
Alternatively,  specific motifs can be provided as a comma separated string. 
Two or more sequential repeats can be required although dimers can be reported as singletons.

This makes it potentially applicable for visualising the distribution of short tandem repeats and other kinds of microsatellites as bed or gff tracks on a reference fasta. For downstream processing of all exact STRs, the underlying python tool ` pytrf `can be run using the `findstr` option, producing either gff, tsv or csv outputs as described at the end of the[ documentation](https://pytrf.readthedocs.io/en/latest).

#### This PR proposes a new tool and suggestions from anyone interested in microsatellites and STRs would be welcomed

Motivation was to recreate some of the [NIH MARBL T2T assembly polishing](https://github.com/marbl/training) browser tracks in Galaxy workflows for the VGP. Those tracks display the density of specific dinucleotides such as `CG` in 128nt windows to help identify problematic regions, where they are over-represented, and may introduce technical errors in alignment for different kinds of sequencing methods. 

The tool can be configured to output all motifs of one or more lengths from 1-6nt.
Alternatively,  specific motifs can be provided as a comma separated string. 
Two or more sequential repeats can be required although dimers can be reported as singletons.

This makes it potentially applicable for visualising the distribution of short tandem repeats and other kinds of microsatellites as bed or gff tracks on a reference fasta. For downstream processing of all exact STRs, the underlying python tool ` pytrf `can be run using the `findstr` option, producing either gff, tsv or csv outputs as described at the end of the[ documentation](https://pytrf.readthedocs.io/en/latest).

#### This PR proposes a new tool and suggestions from anyone interested in microsatellites and STRs would be welcomed

Motivation was to recreate some of the [NIH MARBL T2T assembly polishing](https://github.com/marbl/training) browser tracks in Galaxy workflows for the VGP. Those tracks display the density of specific dinucleotides such as `CG` in 128nt windows to help identify problematic regions, where they are over-represented, and may introduce technical errors in alignment for different kinds of sequencing methods. 

The tool can be configured to output all motifs of one or more lengths from 1-6nt.
Alternatively,  specific motifs can be provided as a comma separated string. 
Two or more sequential repeats can be required although dimers can be reported as singletons.

This makes it potentially applicable for visualising the distribution of short tandem repeats and other kinds of microsatellites as bed or gff tracks on a reference fasta. For downstream processing of all exact STRs, the underlying python tool ` pytrf `can be run using the `findstr` option, producing either gff, tsv or csv outputs as described at the end of the[ documentation](https://pytrf.readthedocs.io/en/latest).

#### This PR proposes a new tool and suggestions from anyone interested in microsatellites and STRs would be welcomed

Motivation was to recreate some of the [NIH MARBL T2T assembly polishing](https://github.com/marbl/training) browser tracks in Galaxy workflows for the VGP. Those tracks display the density of specific dinucleotides such as `CG` in 128nt windows to help identify problematic regions, where they are over-represented, and may introduce technical errors in alignment for different kinds of sequencing methods. 

The tool can be configured to output all motifs of one or more lengths from 1-6nt.
Alternatively,  specific motifs can be provided as a comma separated string. 
Two or more sequential repeats can be required although dimers can be reported as singletons.

This makes it potentially applicable for visualising the distribution of short tandem repeats and other kinds of microsatellites as bed or gff tracks on a reference fasta. For downstream processing of all exact STRs, the underlying python tool ` pytrf `can be run using the `findstr` option, producing either gff, tsv or csv outputs as described at the end of the[ documentation](https://pytrf.readthedocs.io/en/latest).

#### This PR proposes a new tool and suggestions from anyone interested in microsatellites and STRs would be welcomed

Motivation was to recreate some of the [NIH MARBL T2T assembly polishing](https://github.com/marbl/training) browser tracks in Galaxy workflows for the VGP. Those tracks display the density of specific dinucleotides such as `CG` in 128nt windows to help identify problematic regions, where they are over-represented, and may introduce technical errors in alignment for different kinds of sequencing methods. 

The tool can be configured to output all motifs of one or more lengths from 1-6nt.
Alternatively,  specific motifs can be provided as a comma separated string. 
Two or more sequential repeats can be required although dimers can be reported as singletons.

This makes it potentially applicable for visualising the distribution of short tandem repeats and other kinds of microsatellites as bed or gff tracks on a reference fasta. For downstream processing of all exact STRs, the underlying python tool ` pytrf `can be run using the `findstr` option, producing either gff, tsv or csv outputs as described at the end of the[ documentation](https://pytrf.readthedocs.io/en/latest).

#### This PR proposes a new tool and suggestions from anyone interested in microsatellites and STRs would be welcomed

Motivation was to recreate some of the [NIH MARBL T2T assembly polishing](https://github.com/marbl/training) browser tracks in Galaxy workflows for the VGP. Those tracks display the density of specific dinucleotides such as `CG` in 128nt windows to help identify problematic regions, where they are over-represented, and may introduce technical errors in alignment for different kinds of sequencing methods. 

The tool can be configured to output all motifs of one or more lengths from 1-6nt.
Alternatively,  specific motifs can be provided as a comma separated string. 
Two or more sequential repeats can be required although dimers can be reported as singletons.

This makes it potentially applicable for visualising the distribution of short tandem repeats and other kinds of microsatellites as bed or gff tracks on a reference fasta. For downstream processing of all exact STRs, the underlying python tool ` pytrf `can be run using the `findstr` option, producing either gff, tsv or csv outputs as described at the end of the[ documentation](https://pytrf.readthedocs.io/en/latest).

#### This PR proposes a new tool and suggestions from anyone interested in microsatellites and STRs would be welcomed

Motivation was to recreate some of the [NIH MARBL T2T assembly polishing](https://github.com/marbl/training) browser tracks in Galaxy workflows for the VGP. Those tracks display the density of specific dinucleotides such as `CG` in 128nt windows to help identify problematic regions, where they are over-represented, and may introduce technical errors in alignment for different kinds of sequencing methods. 

The tool can be configured to output all motifs of one or more lengths from 1-6nt.
Alternatively,  specific motifs can be provided as a comma separated string. 
Two or more sequential repeats can be required although dimers can be reported as singletons.

This makes it potentially applicable for visualising the distribution of short tandem repeats and other kinds of microsatellites as bed or gff tracks on a reference fasta. For downstream processing of all exact STRs, the underlying python tool ` pytrf `can be run using the `findstr` option, producing either gff, tsv or csv outputs as described at the end of the[ documentation](https://pytrf.readthedocs.io/en/latest).

#### This PR proposes a new tool and suggestions from anyone interested in microsatellites and STRs would be welcomed

Motivation was to recreate some of the [NIH MARBL T2T assembly polishing](https://github.com/marbl/training) browser tracks in Galaxy workflows for the VGP. Those tracks display the density of specific dinucleotides such as `CG` in 128nt windows to help identify problematic regions, where they are over-represented, and may introduce technical errors in alignment for different kinds of sequencing methods. 

The tool can be configured to output all motifs of one or more lengths from 1-6nt.
Alternatively,  specific motifs can be provided as a comma separated string. 
Two or more sequential repeats can be required although dimers can be reported as singletons.

This makes it potentially applicable for visualising the distribution of short tandem repeats and other kinds of microsatellites as bed or gff tracks on a reference fasta. For downstream processing of all exact STRs, the underlying python tool ` pytrf `can be run using the `findstr` option, producing either gff, tsv or csv outputs as described at the end of the[ documentation](https://pytrf.readthedocs.io/en/latest).

#### This PR proposes a new tool and suggestions from anyone interested in microsatellites and STRs would be welcomed

Motivation was to recreate some of the [NIH MARBL T2T assembly polishing](https://github.com/marbl/training) browser tracks in Galaxy workflows for the VGP. Those tracks display the density of specific dinucleotides such as `CG` in 128nt windows to help identify problematic regions, where they are over-represented, and may introduce technical errors in alignment for different kinds of sequencing methods. 

The tool can be configured to output all motifs of one or more lengths from 1-6nt.
Alternatively,  specific motifs can be provided as a comma separated string. 
Two or more sequential repeats can be required although dimers can be reported as singletons.

This makes it potentially applicable for visualising the distribution of short tandem repeats and other kinds of microsatellites as bed or gff tracks on a reference fasta. For downstream processing of all exact STRs, the underlying python tool ` pytrf `can be run using the `findstr` option, producing either gff, tsv or csv outputs as described at the end of the[ documentation](https://pytrf.readthedocs.io/en/latest).

#### This PR proposes a new tool and suggestions from anyone interested in microsatellites and STRs would be welcomed

Motivation was to recreate some of the [NIH MARBL T2T assembly polishing](https://github.com/marbl/training) browser tracks in Galaxy workflows for the VGP. Those tracks display the density of specific dinucleotides such as `CG` in 128nt windows to help identify problematic regions, where they are over-represented, and may introduce technical errors in alignment for different kinds of sequencing methods. 

The tool can be configured to output all motifs of one or more lengths from 1-6nt.
Alternatively,  specific motifs can be provided as a comma separated string. 
Two or more sequential repeats can be required although dimers can be reported as singletons.

This makes it potentially applicable for visualising the distribution of short tandem repeats and other kinds of microsatellites as bed or gff tracks on a reference fasta. For downstream processing of all exact STRs, the underlying python tool ` pytrf `can be run using the `findstr` option, producing either gff, tsv or csv outputs as described at the end of the[ documentation](https://pytrf.readthedocs.io/en/latest).

#### This PR proposes a new tool and suggestions from anyone interested in microsatellites and STRs would be welcomed

Motivation was to recreate some of the [NIH MARBL T2T assembly polishing](https://github.com/marbl/training) browser tracks in Galaxy workflows for the VGP. Those tracks display the density of specific dinucleotides such as `CG` in 128nt windows to help identify problematic regions, where they are over-represented, and may introduce technical errors in alignment for different kinds of sequencing methods. 

The tool can be configured to output all motifs of one or more lengths from 1-6nt.
Alternatively,  specific motifs can be provided as a comma separated string. 
Two or more sequential repeats can be required although dimers can be reported as singletons.

This makes it potentially applicable for visualising the distribution of short tandem repeats and other kinds of microsatellites as bed or gff tracks on a reference fasta. For downstream processing of all exact STRs, the underlying python tool ` pytrf `can be run using the `findstr` option, producing either gff, tsv or csv outputs as described at the end of the[ documentation](https://pytrf.readthedocs.io/en/latest).

Adds an optional descriptive distribution report on each contig for each input bigwig and a test.  Some minor cleanups and an extended version string so new version.

In testing, coverage and dimer bigwig values have *extremely long right tailed* skewed distributions. Report includes a crude ascii histogram. Can help when choosing quantile cutoffs and it is possible to just generate the report without making any beds. Faster.

Where there are millions of zeros, it is hard to find informative `low quantile` regions unless the required run size is large and even then, it may not really be helpful.

The high cutoff in these long right tailed skewed distributions can be adjusted to flag as many outlier regions as wanted, in combination with the required number of repeats

[X] This PR updates an existing tool or tool collection

Adds an optional descriptive distribution report on each contig for each input bigwig and a test.  Some minor cleanups and an extended version string so new version.

In testing, coverage and dimer bigwig values have *extremely long right tailed* skewed distributions. Report includes a crude ascii histogram. Can help when choosing quantile cutoffs and it is possible to just generate the report without making any beds. Faster.

Where there are millions of zeros, it is hard to find informative `low quantile` regions unless the required run size is large and even then, it may not really be helpful.

The high cutoff in these long right tailed skewed distributions can be adjusted to flag as many outlier regions as wanted, in combination with the required number of repeats

In the long run, if the goal is for Galaxy to become a completely generic platform, the built in genomic metadata and converters must eventually become pluggable like everything else?

Use case is VGP workflows where the input assembly is constantly being improved, and a custom genome would need to be manually revised for every assembly update. _Possible_ that this would always be done manually, but fragile and likely to lead to failures from a missing contig in a new assembly...

Update to allow a chromosome length file to be supplied
Test added and dependencies updated to latest versions 

This way can ensure that the contigs and lengths are correct at each workflow run.

as a draft for comment: Should this converter be moved out of the` lib/galaxy/datatypes/converters` built-in tools into an IUC tool?
 
In the long run, **_if_** Galaxy is to become a generic platform for all kinds of open science, all the built in genomic metadata and converters will eventually become pluggable, like everything else?

Currently the tool works if the reference has a built-in or custom genome dbkey. 

Use case is VGP workflows where the reference assembly is constantly being improved until it is finished. A custom genome could work but would need to be manually revised for every assembly update. _Possible_ that this would always be done manually, but fragile and likely to lead to failures from a missing contig in a new assembly so this PR allows a chromosome length file to be supplied. Test added and dependencies updated to latest versions 

This way can generate the len file and be confident that the contigs and lengths are correct at each workflow run.

as a draft for comment: Should this converter be moved out of the` lib/galaxy/datatypes/converters` built-in tools into an IUC tool?
 
In the long run, **_if_** Galaxy is to become a generic platform for all kinds of open science, all the built in genomic metadata and converters will eventually become pluggable, like everything else?

Currently the tool works if the reference has a built-in or custom genome dbkey. 

Use case is VGP workflows where the reference assembly is constantly being improved until it is finished. A custom genome could work but would need to be manually revised for every assembly update. _Possible_ that this would always be done manually, but fragile and likely to lead to failures from a missing contig in a new assembly so this PR allows a chromosome length file to be supplied. Test added and dependencies updated to latest versions 

This way can generate the len file and be confident that the contigs and lengths are correct at each workflow run.

In the long run, **_if_** Galaxy is to become a generic platform for all kinds of open science, all the built in genomic metadata and converters will eventually become pluggable, like everything else?

Currently the tool works if the reference has a built-in or custom genome dbkey. 

Use case is VGP workflows where the reference assembly is constantly being improved until it is finished. This amalgamates and fixes some built-in converters. Advantage is an optional len file so contigs and lengths are correct at each workflow run for an assembly where dbkey makes no real sense yet.

Note that this estimates a bigwig of genome coverage for the intervals in a bed - it ignores the actual bed file score - depth of coverage is what is wanted here. A bed track can be used to inspect scores but these are usually far too big (seen 60M rows) to be useful as JBrowse2 tracks.

https://github.com/galaxyproject/galaxy/pull/18356

Use case is VGP workflows where the reference assembly is constantly being improved until it is finished. A custom genome could work but would need to be manually revised for every assembly update. Possible that this would always be done manually, but fragile and likely to lead to failures from a missing contig in a new assembly so this PR allows a chromosome length file to be supplied. 

This amalgamates and fixes some built-in converters. Based on CONVERTER_bed_gff_or_vcf_to_bigwig_0 - Test added and dependencies updated to latest versions.

Advantage is an optional len file so contigs and lengths are correct at each workflow run for an assembly where dbkey makes no real sense yet.

Note that this estimates a bigwig of genome coverage for the intervals in a bed or gff3 - it ignores bed file scores - depth of coverage is what is wanted here. 

A bed track can be used to inspect scores but this is where the bed has millions of rows and is just too big for scores to be useful as JBrowse2 tracks.

https://github.com/galaxyproject/galaxy/pull/18356

Use case is VGP workflows where the reference assembly is constantly being improved until it is finished. A custom genome could work but would need to be manually revised for every assembly update. Possible that this would always be done manually, but fragile and likely to lead to failures from a missing contig in a new assembly so this PR allows a chromosome length file to be supplied. 

This amalgamates and fixes some built-in converters. Based on CONVERTER_bed_gff_or_vcf_to_bigwig_0 - Test added and dependencies updated to latest versions.

Advantage is an optional len file so contigs and lengths are correct at each workflow run for an assembly where dbkey makes no real sense yet.

Note that this estimates a bigwig of genome coverage for the intervals in a bed or gff3 - it ignores bed file scores - depth of coverage is what is wanted here. 

A bed track can be used to inspect scores but this is where the bed has millions of rows and is just too big for scores to be useful as JBrowse2 tracks.

@bernt-matthias:
> Wondering if we should implement this in separate tools (and maybe join as workflow).

If I thought that, I'd be offering 3 different tools! This makes sense to me as is:

 1. the code is relatively simple 
 2. this will make my life a lot easier for VGP JBrowse2 generating workflows where bigwig is going to be the most widely used track format because they have huge multimillion row gff and bed, and 50GB bams that are far too big and slow to be tracks.
 3. there is already converter that does 3 different inputs - it's broken but it exists - would you argue for breaking it up?
 4. this fixes CONVERTER_bed_gff_or_vcf_to_bigwig_0, but fixes the broken gff conversion and replaces (broken) vcf with bam - so it does what 3 existing built-in converters do.
 5. This is for assemblies where there is no useful dbkey. Use case is VGP workflows where the reference assembly is constantly being improved until it is finished. A custom genome could work but would need to be manually revised for every assembly update. Possible that this would always be done manually, but fragile and likely to lead to failures from a missing contig in a new assembly so this PR allows a chromosome length file to be supplied. 

This amalgamates and fixes some built-in converters. Based on CONVERTER_bed_gff_or_vcf_to_bigwig_0 - Test added and dependencies updated to latest versions.

Advantage is an optional len file so contigs and lengths are correct at each workflow run for an assembly where dbkey makes no real sense yet.

Note that this estimates a bigwig of genome coverage for the intervals in a bed or gff3 - it ignores bed file scores - depth of coverage is what is wanted here. 

A bed track can be used to inspect scores but this is where the bed has millions of rows and is just too big for scores to be useful as JBrowse2 tracks.

Use case is VGP workflows where the reference assembly is constantly being improved until it is finished. A custom genome could work but would need to be manually revised for every assembly update. Possible that this would always be done manually, but fragile and likely to lead to failures from a missing contig in a new assembly so this PR allows a chromosome length file to be supplied. 

This amalgamates and fixes some built-in converters. Based on CONVERTER_bed_gff_or_vcf_to_bigwig_0 - Test added and dependencies updated to latest versions.

Advantage is an optional len file so contigs and lengths are correct at each workflow run for an assembly where dbkey makes no real sense yet.

Note that this estimates a bigwig of genome coverage for the intervals in a bed or gff3 - it ignores bed file scores - depth of coverage is what is wanted here. 

A bed track can be used to inspect scores but this is where the bed has millions of rows and is just too big for scores to be useful as JBrowse2 tracks.

Use case is VGP workflows where the reference assembly is constantly being improved until it is finished. A custom genome could work but would need to be manually revised for every assembly update. Possible that this would always be done manually, but fragile and likely to lead to failures from a missing contig in a new assembly so this PR allows a chromosome length file to be supplied. 

This amalgamates and fixes some built-in converters. Based on CONVERTER_bed_gff_or_vcf_to_bigwig_0 - Test added and dependencies updated to latest versions.

Advantage is an optional len file so contigs and lengths are correct at each workflow run for an assembly where dbkey makes no real sense yet.

Note that this estimates a bigwig of genome coverage for the intervals in a bed or gff3 - it ignores bed file scores - depth of coverage is what is wanted here. 

A bed track can be used to inspect scores but this is where the bed has millions of rows and is just too big for scores to be useful as JBrowse2 tracks.

https://github.com/galaxyproject/galaxy/pull/18356

Use case is VGP workflows where the reference assembly is constantly being improved until it is finished. A custom genome could work but would need to be manually revised for every assembly update. Possible that this would always be done manually, but fragile and likely to lead to failures from a missing contig in a new assembly so this PR allows a chromosome length file to be supplied. 

This amalgamates and fixes some built-in converters. Based on CONVERTER_bed_gff_or_vcf_to_bigwig_0 - Test added and dependencies updated to latest versions.

Advantage is an optional len file so contigs and lengths are correct at each workflow run for an assembly where dbkey makes no real sense yet.

Note that this estimates a bigwig of genome coverage for the intervals in a bed or gff3 - it ignores bed file scores - depth of coverage is what is wanted here. 

A bed track can be used to inspect scores but this is where the bed has millions of rows and is just too big for scores to be useful as JBrowse2 tracks.
